Industry News: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
  • The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
  • Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.

The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.

Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.

Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.

The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.

Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.

Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:.

Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external.

The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life.

Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world.

In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth.

Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths â that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," noted UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.

The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible â it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).

This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.

Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.

There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.

This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.

On the central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts â countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.

And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.

Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.

This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (Â£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.

If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.

Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed.

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.

"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".

That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".

According to recent reports, russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a newly introduced banner".

It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other problems to tackle problems they can't solve alone.

Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.

But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.

On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.

In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.

And some of those were agreed at the talks.

The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits â money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases â will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.

They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.

But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.

What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.

It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.

Renewable energy capacity is expected to grow 60% more over the next six-year period than the previous.

The economics have been changing too.

Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.

As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.

Against the headwinds of inflation newly introduced investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".

Industry observers note that this is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities â this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.

In a recent development, "We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He indicates energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".

That doesn't make COP irrelevant.

Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.

"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".

Many are questioning whether the COP process is fit for purpose.

COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.

For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.

The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2Â°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5Â°C.

Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.

Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.

The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.

Industry observers note that now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".

COP collapses: What's the future for climate action?

The COP summit in Turkey has failed because of a row about even mentioning the cause of climate change. Is there a way the world can move forward with coordinated climate action?

The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.

Sources indicate that it is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.

Industry observers note that on many of the procedural complications Camilla Born spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.

According to recent reports, and there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.

So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.

The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

Breaking: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
  • Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market.
  • Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who notes it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's being called a comeback for the ages.

For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.

Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.

Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who notes it believes he is the right person to lead the company.

So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

Recent findings suggest that but his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.

The manufacturer is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Industry observers note that it was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.

They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The organization became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a upcoming direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation.

Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?

Huang has hailed AI as a "fresh industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable organization and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

Sources indicate that "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".

But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he stated.

Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very crucial to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down.

He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was introduced, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.

The man himself stated he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him.

Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrations.

France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.

President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he states, is to bring down the French Republic.

That's quite a claim â and one that needs examining.

Industry observers note that the unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester.

Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavas.

Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in.

These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU security agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

Industry observers note that the answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks â what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" â have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

In a recent development, it's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

How Ukraine drone attacks on Russian ships unfolded.

Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.

If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.

On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.

This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much â but not all â of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

Watch: CCTV indicates explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile.

Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.

In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.

The three Baltic states â Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania â all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.

There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.

Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.

Hybrid warfare isn't newly introduced but it is on the rise.

It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.

Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted in August by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.

Recent findings suggest that there have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

Tech Report: A fresh approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

It has been revealed that china and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

It has been revealed that the US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, indicates study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

In a recent development, the immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler noted.

Sources indicate that mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

In a recent development, the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

Industry observers note that “You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

In a recent development, “They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, remarked Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the fresh research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

Industry observers note that it also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss organization called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Recent findings suggest that other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

Sources indicate that in reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he mentioned.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team states it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very key in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler mentioned.

Industry observers note that they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

Sources indicate that fluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Recent findings suggest that another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler noted, so it would have to be used carefully.

Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August.
  • Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
  • It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student.

Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.

It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.

"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

Industry observers note that after seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.

But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.

When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.

"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it.".

Okuhle's father, Tuku, indicates he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death.

Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.

She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.

Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.

It is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years as police had stopped releasing this breakdown until now.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.

Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa.

The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confrontÂ widespreadÂ violence against women.

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.

But in places like Kokstad, as well as Kempton Park, in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.

For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.

Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.

Industry observers note that "It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate.".

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.

The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has mentioned there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa.

According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.

This year, Amnesty International mentioned South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".

Tuku notes he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.

Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.

"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us.".

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa noted the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.

Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.

In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.

Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.

The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, states Kamvalethu.

Industry observers note that most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He claims the group will call police when they need back-up.

Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu claims the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.

"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do.".

Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

Kgothatso states she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her.

Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.

She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.

When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she claims he started punching and slapping her.

"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," claims Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso indicates she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.

Industry observers note that she indicates her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.

Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.

In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.

She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.

Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

Zama notes her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles.

In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.

She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

Industry observers note that it was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa.

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'.

Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

It has been revealed that zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.

"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.

Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.

Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.

In a recent development, wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone.".

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe.

#62. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1673 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • According to recent reports, 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report reveals.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

According to recent reports, 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report reveals. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

“The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Industry observers note that jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, noted she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company debuted and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

Recent findings suggest that “Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

In a recent development, mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

According to recent reports, most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

In a recent development, “Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

It has been revealed that however, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply challenges posed a challenge, forcing it to presently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

According to recent reports, “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

“Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” said Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

Industry observers note that sephora introduced its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is right now facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

According to recent reports, the gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a tech giant on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, claims her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high shows the scale of India's climate challenge.

Recent findings suggest that “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann noted. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, indicates the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability problems) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”.

Sources indicate that in the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

#57. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1914 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million consumers a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass people’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million consumers a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass people’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

According to recent reports, multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Tech giant insiders stated the exploits were utilized to spy on customers and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” stated Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg noted a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly people until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the manufacturer only targeted consumers in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they stated.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of customers’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they remarked.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

It has been revealed that google Play is not available in China, and Android consumers in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it stated it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” remarked Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen mentioned. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers remarked.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone consumers are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, mentioned Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he noted.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Recent findings suggest that pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he noted.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to customers’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he stated.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” noted René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Industry observers note that suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread swiftly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a fresh enhancement of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the enhancement, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

Recent findings suggest that the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the tech giant’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to massive data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source noted.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they remarked.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, remarked although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

It has been revealed that the Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” remarked Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

The ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

Sources indicate that “Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

    Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

    📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (494 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.
    • The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data demonstrated with all ballots counted.
    • “We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo mentioned in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

    The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data demonstrated with all ballots counted.

    “We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo mentioned in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

    He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

    Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

    Industry observers note that “We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister said in a speech to party members.

    Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive newly introduced leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

    Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

    While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

    The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

    Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

    Orpo has said he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

    Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

    Industry observers note that the Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

    Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

    That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

    📅 04 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (525 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

    Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

    📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget aims by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
    • Recent findings suggest that sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
    • In a recent development, the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget aims by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

    Recent findings suggest that sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

    In a recent development, the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

    Sources indicate that this resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

    Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

    The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled intends to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

    The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

    “There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” noted Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

    But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

    “There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole said.

    It has been revealed that the euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

    Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

    A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

    Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, remarked he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

    “In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.
