    King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend Molly Meldrum

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (463 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
    • Meldrum's family noted he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
    • The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.

    Meldrum's family noted he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.

    The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.

    Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

    Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.

    Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.

    Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.

    "Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family stated.

    Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.

    He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

    King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".

    On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

    "His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry.".

    Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.

    "As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room.".

    "He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support.".

    Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music.".

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • French government minister Marlene Schiappa has come under fire from members of her own party after appearing on the front cover of Playboy magazine.
    • Schiappa, who has been a government minister since 2017, appeared on the cover of the magazine to accompany a 12-page interview she did on women’s and LGBT rights.
    • According to recent reports, schiappa has been a long-time advocate for women’s rights and was appointed as the country’s first ever Gender Equality Minister in 2017.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    French government minister Marlene Schiappa has come under fire from members of her own party after appearing on the front cover of Playboy magazine.

    Schiappa, who has been a government minister since 2017, appeared on the cover of the magazine to accompany a 12-page interview she did on women’s and LGBT rights. Schiappa, who is the current Minister for the Social Economy and French Associations, was photographed for the cover wearing a white dress.

    According to recent reports, schiappa has been a long-time advocate for women’s rights and was appointed as the country’s first ever Gender Equality Minister in 2017. In this role, she successfully spearheaded a new sexual harassment law which allows for on the spot fines to be issued to men who catcall, harass or follow women on the street.

    Her appearance has drawn criticism from political colleagues including French Prime Minister Elisabeth Borne.

    Borne pulled up Schiappa over the cover, telling her it “wasn’t appropriate, especially during this period,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported Saturday, citing a source close to the prime minister.

    France is currently in the throes of a political and social crisis triggered by French President Emmanuel Macron’s move to push ahead with controversial pension reforms despite widespread public opposition.

    “We are in the middle of a social crisis, there is the issue of policing, there are people between life and death, and I have the impression of being behind a smoke screen,” Sandrine Rousseau, Green Party politician and fellow women’s rights activist, told BFMTV Friday.

    France wracked by more pension protests amid rising violence on the streets.

    French politician, Jean Luc Mélenchon who came third in the 2022 presidential elections criticized both Schiappa’s appearance and the decision by French President Emmanuel Macron to give an interview to children’s magazine, Pif Gadget, this week.

    “In a country where the President expresses himself in Pif and his minister in Playboy, the problem would be the opposition. France is going off the rails,” Mélenchon tweeted Saturday.

    Recent findings suggest that schiappa responded to her critics in a tweet on Saturday, saying: “Defending the right of women to have control of their bodies, that’s everywhere and all the time. In France, women are free. With all due respect to the detractors and hypocrites.”.

    French Interior Minister, Gérald Darmanin came to Schiappa’s defense during an interview with French news channel CNews on Sunday calling her a “woman of character.”.

    “I wanted to say that Marlene Schiappa is a courageous female politician who has her character and who has her style which is not mine, but I respect,” he remarked.

    Watch: Carney and Trump impersonators take stage with real Mark Carney.

    Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.

    The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.

    Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.

    "We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator stated after he walked on stage.

    Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.

    "I'm so popular we just had a significant BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator noted at the Saturday press gala.

    According to recent reports, he also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy.".

    There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.

    "I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

    Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its newly introduced interior decorator.".

    Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.

    The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump.

    They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., external.

    Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.

    In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

    According to recent reports, "Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour mentioned.

    Tech Report: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina notes she prepares to return on 16 December

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024.
    • Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has mentioned she aims to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
    • Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024.

    Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has mentioned she aims to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.

    Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.

    The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

    But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.

    Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.

    "Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.

    Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

    India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ârequest for comment. In April, âthe ministry said it was â examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the latest government and further strengthen bilateral ties".

    Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

    What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.

    On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

    "Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.

    According to recent reports, the choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

    Industry observers note that abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.

    Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.

    The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

    The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.

    But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.

    Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

    "I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.

    Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

    India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a newly introduced government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.

    It has been revealed that but nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.

    Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.

    The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

    #38. Industry News: The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

    📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1082 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

    📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
    • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
    • Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

    The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

    Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had launched aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

    Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

    Hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a upcoming class of NASA astronauts.

    He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

    Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

    Industry observers note that “It’s so much more than the four names that have been announced,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

    According to recent reports, glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

    Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which introduced to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

    Recent findings suggest that koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

    The Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

    If all goes to plan, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

    The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

    The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton said via email.

    After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

    Artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

    The Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

    NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already remarked delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

    The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

    In a recent development, vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

    “I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche said. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

    Koch said in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

    “We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch said. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

    She said the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

    An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

    CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024.
    • A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
    • Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024.

    A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

    Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

    Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

    This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

    In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

    At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers noted.

    There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

    On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

    "We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he mentioned.

    "The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately.".

    Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

    "Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," remarked Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

    Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

    In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

    Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

    Industry observers note that since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

    In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.

    Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

    According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.

    Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

    Andrei Chibis's wife rejects the allegations and he is expected to appear in court on Thursday.

    The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.

    Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; Â£9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.

    Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.

    He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis remarked "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".

    In a post on social media, she mentioned her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now.".

    Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.

    Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

    The port of Murmansk is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

    Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.

    However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

    The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.

    Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.

    According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.

    #30. Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

    📅 04 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1367 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

    Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

    📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China debuted last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.
    • At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.
    • It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China debuted last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

    At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

    It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

    This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

    It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

    A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

    But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

    “This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” noted Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

    That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

    The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

    According to recent reports, “Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

    The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

    Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over concerns from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

    According to recent reports, taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

    But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

    Sources indicate that for Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

    That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

    China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

    China thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't.

    The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

    That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”.

    It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

    Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

    While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

    Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

    Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

    Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

    A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

    Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

    This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

    But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

    As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

    It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

    Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” mentioned Sung, the political scientist.

    What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions.

    China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

    Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

    This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an key opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

    An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

    “(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

    “A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”.

    CNN’s Wayne Chang contributed reporting.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Congolese rebels mentioned they had targeted a warplane preparing to bomb the town of Minembwe.

    The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.

    Industry observers note that the military noted it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.

    On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) remarked it had shot down a plane of the same type that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.

    Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is stated to have been captured alive.

    On Tuesday, the FRN noted the plane they had shot down was a Cessna 208, which had been "converted into a light attack aircraft" enabling it "to carry and launch precision-guided bombs and missiles".

    Its wreckage now lies 10km (6 miles) from Minembwe, a rebel statement said.

    The BBC has not independently verified the rebel claim, or whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one the rebels say they shot down.

    Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.

    What's the fighting in DR Congo all about?

    How former President Kabila became FRN rebel leader.

    Sources indicate that A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X mentioned: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company.".

    The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.

    Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".

    Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.

    In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.

    He and the alleged South African pilot are stated to be the only other survivors.

    South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".

    "Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.

    In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.

    The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.

    In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.

    The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.

    Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.

    Over the weekend, medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res stated fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.

    The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

    The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

    #27. Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

    📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (662 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

    Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

    📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
    • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
    • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person stated, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

    The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

    Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person stated, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

    A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical latest insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

    The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

    As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it claims is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

    The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

    CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the latest intelligence.

    In a recent development, the balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

    A senior State Department official noted in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

    It has been revealed that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, mentioned at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

    The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

    Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

    China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

    It has been revealed that still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

    This story has been updated with additional reporting.

    CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

    • A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.
    • The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The explosion ripped through one of the city's central squares.

    A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.

    The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.

    No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

    Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details. Armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by De la Espriella.

    Writing on social media, the president stated that his government would "bluntly and forcefully" respond, external to "every drop of Colombian blood spilled".

    "There will be no impunity and no retreat," he added.

    It is the latest in a series of attacks targeting official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

    Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province.

    And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of CÃºcuta.

    The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.

    Following the signing of the deal, thousands of left-wing rebel fighters laid down their arms.

    However, a significant number of Farc members, who did not agree with the deal, refused to disarm and joined dissident groups instead.

    While forced displacement, child recruitment and the numbers of attacks on security forces dropped in the aftermath of the deal, there has been an upsurge in recent years driven by dissident Farc factions and criminal groups fighting for control of drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion rackets.

    Colombia's first left-wing president, who was in power from August 2022 to August 2026, tried to negotiate with these armed groups as part of what he called his "total peace" strategy.

    However, the talks stalled and collapsed with several of the criminal groups violating ceasefires they had agreed to observe.

    De la Espriella was elected on a promise to crack down on "narcoterrorism" and has been scathing about his predecessor's approach.

    He has also been critical of the 2016 agreement, calling it a "false peace".

    In a post on X, uploaded shortly before news of the car bomb in Villavicencio spread, he referred to the peace deal as a "mess", describing it as a "waste of public resources" and the "cause behind Colombia's ruin".

    Former President Juan Manuel Santos and Rodrigo LondoÃ±o - the two men who signed the peace deal on behalf of the Colombian government and the Farc respectively - defended it in an interview with BBC Mundo ahead of the anniversary.

    Santos said that De la Espriella was "totally wrong" to call it a "false peace".

    "He wants to use, or has bought into that cynical and mistaken theory that the violence we see today is the result of the peace deal, when the exact opposite is the case," Santos mentioned, arguing that the problem lies with the lack of implementation of the agreement.

    GisÃ¨le Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.

    The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

    Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

    The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

    Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes.".

    "Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she noted.

    The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

    French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.

    In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

    In a recent development, "We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms GisÃ¨le Pelicot," it said. The manufacturer also apologised to the author.

    Tinbad remarked "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.

    French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".

    "These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it stated.

    Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".

    Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.

    Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

    After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.

    Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

    If you have been affected by the complications in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

    Breaking: Pope Francis' diary reveals claims he saw the devil three times

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.
    • In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.
    • "I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.

    In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.

    "I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.

    In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.

    Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign.

    "Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry.

    "It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious.".

    Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes.

    "He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he mentioned happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.

    He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome.

    "I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything," he wrote, adding that "the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters".

    The collection of diaries was edited by a longtime friend of Francis.

    The late pope also revealed that while getting ready to go to sleep in June 2018, he "saw the gates of hell".

    "I watched a little, and it terrified me," he stated, adding that he "took the rosary as a weapon".

    "It's dangerous to get close to the gates of hell, because flames can spring out and burn," he wrote.

    Cardinal Victor Fernandez, head of the Vatican's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and friend of Francis, edited the diaries, which are the first by a pope to be released to the public since the 1960s.

    Pope Francis was elected pope in 2013 and died aged 88 in April 2025.

    Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A funeral was held earlier in southern Gaza for three Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike.
    • At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.
    • Recent findings suggest that naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A funeral was held earlier in southern Gaza for three Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike.

    At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.

    Recent findings suggest that naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.

    Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz revealed that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.

    The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.

    Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

    Industry observers note that gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.

    The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.

    Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.

    Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.

    The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".

    It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".

    Gaza's interior ministry mentioned Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "key achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".

    Gaza's health ministry warned that there was a rapid rise in cases of meningitis in October.

    Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

    At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

    Israel indicates six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

    The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.

    The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.

    On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.

    Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it stated.

    Israeli military body Cogat stated on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.

    The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

    Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry indicates.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Saurav Das remarked that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK.

    One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has noted the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.

    Saurav Das noted he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.

    In an interview with the BBC, Das noted there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on concerns that matter to young people.

    The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

    Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident revealed the government was "scared".

    "They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them.".

    By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.

    According to recent reports, "It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this reveals Prime Minister Modi in such poor light.

    "It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government.".

    Saurav Das (L) speaking following the resignation of India's education minister in July.

    Das mentioned he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.

    Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country.".

    On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".

    Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.

    In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

    Industry observers note that in October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

    The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

    Das insisted the CJP would continue protesting, but it did not want to be a political party "as of today".

    "It's a long haul. We are not here for a short time. We are looking at India in the next 10 to 20 years. How do we develop India into a better country? That is the vision that we want to carry forward.".

    Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.

    There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.

    In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

    Industry observers note that in March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

    Additional reporting by Cherylann Mollan.

    After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty.

    #11. Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (776 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Syrians coming back after the war are falling victim to mines and other explosives.
    • Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
    • "Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Syrians coming back after the war are falling victim to mines and other explosives.

    Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.

    "Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.

    Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

    Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.

    The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).

    The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.

    According to recent reports, alaa's father mentioned demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.

    But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

    "Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.

    The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

    A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.

    Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.

    The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

    "When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins stated.

    More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.

    "They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation.".

    Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.

    Recent findings suggest that they have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.

    But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.

    Both government forces and rebels laid land mines during the civil war.

    For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.

    Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.

    More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.

    The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.

    Sources indicate that in one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.

    The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.

    The Syrian Ministry of Defence indicates since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.

    But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.

    "We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins mentioned.

    And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.

    Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus.

    Syrians struggle with soaring prices as crisis challenges post-Assad recovery.

Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

    In a recent development, coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

    Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space.
    • Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
    • Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space.

    Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

    Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

    German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said such reports were "not fresh, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously".

    Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

    The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

    Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper SÃ¼ddeutscher Zeitung, remarked the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including crucial communication and observation satellites.

    Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element.".

    The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, said Rutte.

    "When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary.".

    Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but stated they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

    German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

    Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario".

    Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit.

    According to recent reports, bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, noted that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure".

    Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or strategy to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

    It has been revealed that in 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.

    According to recent reports, "Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin stated at the time.

    In a recent development, in September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".
